title: VC0-02466
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) is a citizen of Angola and a permanent resident of Brazil. Her daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant) is a citizen of Brazil. Ms. XXXX fears religious persecution and sexual violence in Angola, where she was sexually assaulted by a security guard. She lived in Brazil from 2012 to 2019 and has permanent residence there. Her husband, who is from the Democratic Republic of Congo, has Brazilian citizenship. On one occasion, the couple was robbed and assaulted. Subsequently, the husband and her son were kidnapped by Kabila supporters in Brazil due to her husband's political views. Ms. XXXX fears that the kidnappers will target her and her minor daughter due to their family connection and imputed political opinions if they return to Brazil. Both Appellants fear political opponents of their husband in Brazil who kidnapped and harmed members of the family. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellants were excluded under Article 1E of the Convention1 and that their claim lacked credibility. I agree that exclusion and credibility are the determinative issues.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected

According to the law,2 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.3

The Appellants have submitted the Basis of Claims and narratives from their husband/father and son/brother as new evidence. Those claims are being decided separately as the men made their claims after the RPD decided the Appellants' claims. Although these narratives were completed after the Appellants' RPD hearing, the events that they describe arose before the RPD made its decision and are another chronicle of the events at the heart of the Appellants' claims. The Appellants' explanation that "the documents provide supporting evidence" is inadequate as it does not explain how the evidence meets the statutory criteria. I also note that the Appellants already provided letters from the husband at the RPD hearing. In her Affidavit, Ms. XXXX indicates that she "attended the RPD hearing with the documents that she had" suggesting that her new evidence is documentary evidence that was previously unavailable to her. She also indicates that her husband and son amended their narratives as their accounts had the omissions and contradictions identified in the Appellants' narratives. I find that the Basis of Claims forms are essentially a retelling of the Appellants' initial claim. An appeal before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is not an opportunity for an appellant to augment the record they presented at the RPD and simply address errors or gaps in their evidence. I find that the Basis of Claim does not meet the criteria for new evidence and is not admissible.

The Appellants have also provided an affidavit from Ms. XXXX. This affidavit relates the problems which lead to the delays in perfecting her appeal views and her views about the RPD decision but does not contain new facts or other evidence. I have considered this affidavit as part of the Appellants' memorandum of argument.

The Appellants are requesting an oral hearing under section 110(6) of the Act.4 As I have not found that there is admissible new evidence which relates to the credibility of the Appellants, I find that there is no jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5 The Appellants allege that the RPD erred in the following findings: a. that the Appellants lacked credibility because of the inconsistencies in their testimony; b. that the Appellants omitted material relevant and important information in their Basis of Claim form (BOC); c. that the Appellants lacked credibility because their supporting letters did not mention that their husband and son had been kidnapped and released; and d. that the Appellants were excluded under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention.

I have also considered this claim in light of the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.6 In this case, Ms. XXXX is a survivor of sexual and physical assaults.

Finally, I have been mindful that Ms. XXXX was unrepresented at the RPD hearing. I have assessed this claim in light of Ms. XXXX education and background. In addition, I am cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, testifying over a video call, testifying through an interpreter and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions. Exclusion

The Chair of the IRB issued a jurisprudential guide for cases involving an analysis of exclusion under Article 1E.7 The jurisprudential guide involves a Haitian man who had permanent residency in Brazil and feared harm from a Brazilian criminal gang. He also alleged that there was discrimination against Haitians in Brazil. I find that the Jurisprudential Guide is applicable to this case as both cases involve permanent residency in Brazil, both cases allege specific harm from criminality as well as discrimination in Brazil based on race. I acknowledge the present case also involves a fear of gender-based violence, a claim based on Convention8 grounds of imputed political opinion and family connection and the claim of a minor child which are all factors which are not considered in the Jurisprudential Guide. Consistent with the IRB's Policy on the Use of Jurisprudential Guides9, I will be using the reasoning in the guide as a preferred interpretation of the conflicting Federal Court caselaw in exclusion cases. Consistent with the Jurisprudential Guide, I must assess, with respect to Brazil, Ms. XXXX situation on the same day that the RPD considered it, being the day of the RPD hearing. To determine whether the exclusion clause in section 98 of the Act is applicable, I must determine whether, on the day of the hearing, Ms. XXXX had status that was substantially similar to that of Brazilian nationals. If the answer is yes, I must determine whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the Ms. XXXX prospective risk as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection in Brazil.10 In this later analysis, I have considered the Appellants' specific claim based on the events involving their family in Brazil and their residual profile.

The RPD found that Ms. XXXX was excluded as she had status in Brazil which granted them rights and responsibilities similar to those of citizens of that country. Having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that the RPD did not err in this finding.

To be subject to exclusion under section 98 of the Act, the refugee protection claimant must enjoy substantially the same rights and responsibilities as nationals. The right to return, the right to work freely without restrictions, the right to study, and the right to social services and health care are some of the rights which can be considered in this analysis. The minor Appellant is a citizen of Brazil by virtue of her birth in Brazil.11 The evidence also shows that Ms. XXXX had permanent resident status in Brazil.12

Ms. XXXX testified that she had worked in Brazil in a XXXX and as a XXXX. She also testified that she would be able to study or to get public health services in Brazil. She also testified that she could return to Brazil, which is consistent with the Permanent Resident status listed on her identification documents.13 The Brazilian constitution guarantees that foreigners living in Brazil will have the same rights as Brazilian citizens in terms of access to health care, education, social services and security, although it sets out restrictions to the right to vote, to carry out military service and to hold certain public offices.14 The NDP further indicates that Brazilian law prohibits discrimination on the basis of race in employment, housing and public services and includes criminal sanctions for crimes motivated by racial prejudice.15

The documentary evidence indicates that individuals may lose permanent resident status if they have been absent from the country for more than two years.16 The evidence on the record leads me to conclude that, on the day of the RPD hearing, Ms. XXXX had valid permanent resident status in Brazil and had the right to return. Discrimination

The RPD found that Ms. XXXX residual profile as a woman of colour in Brazil and her daughter's residual profile as a young girl in Brazil did not amount to persecution. The objective evidence is "darker-skinned citizens, especially Afro-Brazilians, encountered discrimination" including in government employment, lower wages, unemployment and higher rates of poverty. "The statistics disaggregated by race widely available throughout Brazil demonstrate a consistent socioeconomic gap between blacks and whites due to discrimination in every aspect of society."17

Discrimination rises to the level of persecution where there are a number of discriminatory acts substantially prejudicial to the person concerned, which takes place in a general atmosphere of insecurity and which result in a feeling of apprehension and insecurity about the future existence of the person concerned.18 An examination of whether discrimination rises to persecution must always take into account the personal circumstances and vulnerabilities of the Appellant.19

The objective evidence indicates that gender violence has epidemic proportions in Brazil, with the country ranked fifth in the world for its levels of femicide. The rates of sexual violence against young girls is particularly shocking in Brazil: four girls under the age of 13 years are sexually assaulted every hour in Brazil. The evidence also shows that the Brazilian government and civil society have taken many and varied actions to counter this problem: a specific Gender Violence Statute, the criminalization of femicide, preventive programs in schools and social campaigns, and a network of specialized services.20 The evidence also shows that gender violence is predominantly intimate partner violence, which has not been alleged in the Appellants' situation. Police and judges are now paying attention to femicide which may explain some of the increased counting of these crimes.21 Public awareness has increased government attention and marches in major cities have denounced the high rates of gender violence and femicide.

I have also considered the factors set out in various Federal Court decisions on discrimination rising to the level of persecution. First, the decision-maker must consider the situation in the country and whether the government is creating an atmosphere of intolerance.22 In considering the country conditions, the claimant or appellant must establish some link to the objective evidence.23 Second, the decision-maker must consider the consequences of discrimination, including whether there are impacts on an ability to access education and jobs which lead to an insecure future existence.24 Third, the decision-maker must consider the personal circumstances of the appellants and their vulnerabilities, including age, health, finances and gender.25 Finally, the decision-maker must look at the cumulative nature of the discrimination and not consider each factor in its own silo.26

The Appellants have not indicated that they encountered discriminatory acts based on their race or their gender. Based on the objective evidence, I find that the government is not creating an atmosphere of insecurity given their legislative and programming efforts. I also find that the increased public attention to femicide and gender violence leads to the idea that there is not an insecure future existence. I have no information about the Appellants' ability to access jobs or education. While I accept the evidence that there is discrimination against Afro-Brazilians, I find that this discrimination does not rise to the level of persecution for the Appellants. Moreover, "country conditions alone are insufficient to ground a claim".27 Credibility

The next step in the analysis of this claim is to determine whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellants' risk in Brazil. The RPD made the following findings about credibility: a. The PA testified that her husband and son were released by their captors on XXXX XXXX, 2019, but this information was omitted from her BOC even though it occurred prior to her signature of the BOC. Her explanation that she did not find out until XXXX 2019 that her husband and son had been released does not explain why her BOC was not amended prior to the start of the hearing or why she did not mention this fact at the hearing. b. At the port-of-entry, Ms. XXXX indicated that she was divorced and had permission to travel with her daughter. She did not say that her husband and son had been kidnapped. At the RPD hearing, Ms. XXXX denied telling CBSA that she was divorced. c. Two of her support letters, including the one from her husband, did not mention the husband being kidnapped for XXXX months. d. The RPD accepted her allegation she and her husband were robbed in XXXX 2019 but found that this robbery was a result of generalized criminality, being a general risk in Brazil.

The RPD found that there were several important omissions and contradictions between Ms. XXXX testimony at the border, her narrative and her oral testimony. I have been mindful of the caselaw about the use of statements made at the border. For example, as the role of the immigration officer is to determine whether an individual is eligible and/or admissible to initiate a refugee claim, one should not expect port of entry notes to contain all of the details of the claim.28 On the other hand, the Federal Court has held that "contradictions between an applicant's testimony, port of entry statements and PIF, as well as the omission of elements in the PIF, crucial to his or her claim, may legitimately serve as a basis for a negative credibility finding."29

In order to assess credibility based on omissions and contradictions in the port of entry notes, the Federal Court has explained that "[t]he nature and significance of the applicants' contradiction or omission in the immigration officer's notes at the port of entry and their PIFs must therefore be assessed."30 Omissions and contradictions which have been found to meet this threshold include those that are real,31 significant,32 and concern elements that are crucial,33 essential,34 or central to the claim.35 A claimant's credibility can be impugned solely on the basis of contradictions stemming from the port of entry notes that meet these requirements.36

I find that the omission of the language spoken by the men who robbed Ms. XXXX and her husband is not a crucial or essential detail upon which the Appellants' credibility can be impugned. I agree with the Appellants' argument that the stress and trauma may have affected the husband's recall of the robbery. I also note the Appellants' argument that there are increasing numbers of Congolese people living in Brazil, however, this fact doesn't help me to decide, one way or the other, whether the assailants spoke Lingala or whether the language of the assailants means that the attack was politically motivated or generalized crime.

I also find that the RPD was incorrect about Ms. XXXX omission of the release of her husband and son. The RPD found that Ms. XXXX could have amended her narrative prior to the hearing or could have proactively testified to the release of her husband and son. I disagree with those two findings. I find that it is possible, on a balance of probabilities, that an unrepresented claimant testifying through an interpreter would not have had the presence of mind to indicate this important change at the beginning of the hearing or to amend her written narrative.

However, I find that the RPD's other findings on credibility were correct. The omission of injuries to her four-year-old son is a significant detail. I am not persuaded by her explanations that she was advised to include only a brief summary of her claim in her written evidence.

I also agree with the RPD's finding about Ms. XXXX marital status. Given that the claims of both Appellants are linked to their ties to their husband or father, the claim of being married or divorced is more than a nuance and a misunderstanding. I am mindful that the Federal Court has indicated that port of entry interviews must be taken with some reticence given the circumstances in which the interviews are made, for example as claimants are without counsel and may be physically or mentally exhausted from their travel.37 On the other hand, the Federal Court has also found that port of entry notes can be relied on due to the officer's lack of interest in the outcome and the contemporaneous nature of the notes.38 I find that the distinction between being married and being divorced is important, for a border official considering the admissibility of a woman travelling with a child, would be looking for a potential child abduction or other similarly serious issues. I find that Ms. XXXX was not truthful about her marital status at the border and that this affects the credibility of her claim.

I also find that the omission of the kidnapping from the port of entry notes is significant. The notes indicate that Ms. XXXX said her husband and son "had some trouble" which would explain why they were not travelling with the Appellants. The vagueness of this description weakens the credibility of the Appellants' claim that they were fleeing Brazil based on the kidnapping of their family members. The kidnapping is the central tenant of the Appellants' claim: to have described it as "some trouble" belies the credibility of their account. I find that these two omissions impugn the credibility of the Appellants' account.

I note that the Appellants are not contesting the RPD's findings about the omission in the letters of support and having reviewed those letters find that the RPD's findings are correct. The omission of kidnapping from the letter from Mr. XXXX is an important detail. I agree with the RPD's general finding that the kidnapping of her husband and son did not happen.

I agree with the RPD's finding that the robbery of Ms. XXXX and her husband in Brazil reflects a generalized risk of crime to which all Brazilians are subject. Ms. XXXX has not provided any evidence to contest this finding and having reviewed the record, I find that the RPD is correct.

Finally, I have specifically considered the claim of Ms. XXXX XXXX who is currently a minor. Ms. XXXX indicates that her daughter would be at risk from the same criminals who kidnapped her husband and son. As I have found that the kidnapping did not happen, I find that there is no risk to Ms. XXXX XXXX on this basis.

I have also considered the argument that Ms. XXXX XXXX is at risk as a young Black girl in Brazil. The objective evidence points to a wave of public anger about the high rates of crimes against women. The objective evidence also shows that "femicide and other forms of violence against women is extremely high, disproportionately affecting young, black women."39 However, these are not crimes against very young girls but are crimes against women in their young adulthood and are largely crimes related to intimate partner violence. When it comes to social and economic conditions, 70% of those living in extreme poverty are Afro-Brazilian. They earn less money, have higher rates of illiteracy and their education levels are lower. Afro-Brazilian women in particular are marginalized and disadvantaged, more likely to experience violence, overrepresented in low-skilled jobs and overrepresented in prison populations.40 The objective evidence also points to the Brazilian government's efforts to combat racism, with specialized programs, development funds, increased minimum wages, and affirmative action programs.41 Not all discriminatory acts amount to persecution42 and the objective evidence suggests a willingness on the part of the Brazilian government to remedy the social and economic status of Afro-Brazilians. While I accept the evidence that there is discrimination against Afro-Brazilians, I find that this discrimination does not rise to the level of persecution for the Appellants. As I have found for Ms. XXXX, I find that the level of discrimination to which Ms. XXXX XXXX may be subject based on her residual profile does not rise to the level of persecution.

I find that Ms. XXXX is excluded from the definition of a Convention refugee or person in need of protection pursuant to Article 1E of the Convention. Based on my review of the totality of the oral and written evidence, I also find that neither Appellant has established that they face a forward-looking risk as Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, I dismiss the appeals of XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
